THE CO-OPTING OF THE BUDDHIST: THE IPVV AGAINST VIJÑĀNAVĀDA AND DHARMAKĪRTI

Two idealisms, one starting point — the dream-inversion, the other-minds refutation, and the valence of the same appearances

  • magnum-opus essay. 2026-08-11. The Pratyabhijñā and the Buddhist idealists (the Vijñānavādins, and
  • eir Dharmakīrtian epistemology) are the two great idealisms of India. Both hold that appearances
  • bhāsa) are all we have — that the world is, in some sense, consciousness. But they draw opposite
  • nclusions: the Buddhist reads the appearances as unreal (no-self, empty), the Śaiva reads them as the
  • al self-articulation of consciousness. This essay is the complete comparative synthesis of the two,
  • ntered on the IPVV's method of co-opting — its acceptance and inversion of the Buddhist's own tools.
  • expounds the co-opting pattern (the inference-theory, the dream, self-awareness), the
  • eam-inversion (the deepest move), the other-minds refutation, and the honest check (does the co-opting
  • uggle the conclusion?). It is grounded in the IPVV's L2 layer (V2E, V2F, V2G, V2C) and the
  • shing-ipvv sessions, and it is now possible in full because the IPVV is translated.*

PART I — THE TWO IDEALISMS

1.1 The Buddhist idealisms

  • e Vijñānavādins (the Yogācāra, the "mind-only" school) hold that the world is, in its essence,
  • nsciousness — that objects are forms (ākāra) of cognition, not external things. Their epistemology
  • aches its peak in Dharmakīrti, who systematizes the inference-theory (the hetu), the apoha (the
  • clusion-theory of concepts), and the svasamvedana (self-awareness).
  • e Buddhist idealist's structure:
  • `
  • gnition with its form (ākāra) — the blue-form
  • the world (no external object)
  • momentary, self-contained, without a Self
  • `
  • e Buddhist reads the appearances negatively: they are unreal (no external thing), empty (no Self),
  • d momentary (no persistence).

1.2 The Pratyabhijñā (the recognition school)

  • e Pratyabhijñā, founded by Utpaladeva and systematized by Abhinavagupta, also holds that the world is
  • nsciousness — that objects are forms of cognition, not external things. But it draws the opposite
  • nclusion from the shared starting point.
  • e Śaiva's structure:
  • `
  • gnition with its form (the blue-form)
  • the world (no external object, but the object is REAL as the ground of the form)
  • the self-articulation of consciousness (the object is the reflection's ground)
  • one free, self-aware consciousness (the Lord)
  • `
  • e Śaiva reads the appearances positively: they are the real self-articulation of consciousness.

1.3 The question of the comparison

  • e two idealisms share the starting point — appearances (ābhāsa) as all we have. Neither posits an
  • knowable external thing as primary. And they diverge on the valence given to the appearances:
  • The Buddhist reads them negatively: unreal, no-self, empty, momentary.
  • The Śaiva reads them positively: the real self-articulation of consciousness, self-aware, free.
  • The thesis of this essay.* The IPVV's method against the Buddhist is *co-opting — it does not
  • fute the Buddhist's premises but accepts them and shows they lead to the Śaiva conclusion. This is the
  • epest thing about the Śaiva-Buddhist relation: it is not a clash of worldviews but a dispute over the
  • lence of the same appearances. And the comparison reveals the honest boundary: the co-opting
  • lidly blocks the Buddhist's negative conclusion, but it smuggles the positive universalization.

PART II — THE CO-OPTING PATTERN

2.1 The co-opting moves (the gems)

  • e pushing-ipvv session on the Buddhist co-opting surfaced four moves where the IPVV accepts the
  • ddhist's own tools and turns them to the Śaiva conclusion:
  • V2E (the external-object inference): the Vijñānavādin uses the reflection (pratibimba) to infer
  • external ground. Abhinavagupta KEEPS the inference-structure but changes its conclusion: "even
  • e error, being a relation, is a pramā" — the determination of the external is valid *by its bond
  • the thing*. The Buddhist's own inference-theory is used to establish the real object.
  • V2F (the other-minds inference): the Buddhist hopes to infer another's mind (the other stream).
  • hinavagupta uses the Buddhist's OWN inference-rules (the candana/agni fragrance; the
  • eing-gone-to-the-other" as un-inferable) to show the inference fails. Then: "the appearances alone
  • ffice" — the ābhāsa is real and enough.
  • V2G (the dream): the Buddhist (Yogācāra) says the world is like a dream (unreal). Abhinavagupta
  • REES the world is like a dream — but draws the OPPOSITE conclusion: the dream proves the
  • nsciousness CREATES the object-mass by its will, without a material cause. The Buddhist's own
  • ample is inverted.
  • V2C (self-luminous cognition): the Buddhist's own svasamvedana (self-awareness) is adopted and
  • epened — cognition is self-luminous and never the object of another.

2.2 The pattern, stated

  • ross all four, the pattern is the same: **Abhinavagupta does not attack the Buddhist's premises; he
  • CEPTS them and shows they lead to the Śaiva conclusion.** The inference-theory, the dream, the
  • lf-awareness — all the Buddhist's own principles — are used to establish consciousness as fundamental
  • d creative.

2.3 Why the co-opting works (the structural reason)

  • e co-opting succeeds because the two systems share the starting point. Both begin from appearances
  • bhāsa) as all we have. The Buddhist concludes: therefore there is only the inner cognition (idealism).
  • e Śaiva takes the SAME starting point and concludes: therefore the appearances are the
  • lf-articulation of consciousness, and consciousness is real and creative.
  • The difference is not the starting point but the VALENCE given to the appearances** — unreal
  • pearances (Buddhist) vs. the real self-manifestation of consciousness (Śaiva). The co-opting shows
  • e starting point is SHARED — and the difference is the valence, not the data.

PART III — THE DREAM-INVERSION (THE DEEPEST CO-OPTING)

3.1 The Buddhist's dream

  • e Buddhist Yogācāra uses the dream as the model of illusion. In the dream, the jar appears without
  • e clay-wheel-stick lineage of causes; so the world, like the dream, appears without a real external
  • use — and is therefore unreal. The dream is the proof of unreality.

3.2 The inversion

  • hinavagupta AGREES the dream is uncaused. But he asks: what does the dream prove?
"The dream proves that the consciousness alone can create an object-mass, by its will, without a
material cause." (V2G)
  • e dream does not prove the world is unreal; it proves that consciousness creates. The yogin who
  • eates an army or a city by mere will is the proof. And "the Lord manifests the whole world from within
  • mself, by his own will, exactly as a yogin does."
  • The inversion is complete.** The Buddhist's own example of unreality (the dream) is turned into the
  • oof of the creation-power. The dream-jar, the yogin's army — the Buddhist's examples of illusion —
  • come the proofs that consciousness is the sole creator.

3.3 The force of the inversion

  • e dream-inversion is the deepest co-opting because it is a complete reversal of the Buddhist's own
  • idence. The Buddhist marshals the dream for unreality; the IPVV re-reads it as the evidence for the
  • eation-power. The very same phenomenon — the uncaused appearance — supports two opposite conclusions,
  • cause the question is not whether the appearance is uncaused but what that reveals: an unreal
  • pearance (Buddhist) or a creative consciousness (Śaiva).

PART IV — THE OTHER-MINDS REFUTATION

4.1 The Buddhist's escape

  • e Buddhist hopes to escape solipsism by inferring another's mind — from Maitra's speech, his uttered
  • rds and gestures, one can infer what is going on in his mind, the other stream.

4.2 The refutation (V2F)

  • hinavagupta shows the inference cannot work, using the Buddhist's own inference-rules:
  • The candana/agni example.** To infer the fire in the sandalwood from the smoke, you must set aside the
  • ndalwood's fragrance — the mark that this smoke comes from sandalwood. Without it you establish only
  • re in general. To infer another's mind, you would need exactly such a further distinction — the
  • eing-gone-to-the-other," the fact that this utterance belongs to Maitra and not to you. And that
  • nnot be inferred from the mere utterance.
  • The samīhitā-niyama.* Only the *aimed action is the wish's effect. A wish produces the action it
  • tends, not a mere utterance that could be aimed at anything. So from Maitra's utterance one cannot
  • fer his wish. If the mere utterance sufficed, even the piśāca-like case would have to be established
  • his intent, which is absurd.

4.3 The conclusion

  • e other-stream cannot be inferred. And then the co-opting: "the appearances alone suffice" (kārikā 6).
  • do not need a hidden external object or a separate stream behind the appearances; the ābhāsa is real
  • d enough. The Buddhist's own inference-theory, used to reach the other, is turned to show the
  • pearances suffice — the Śaiva conclusion.

PART V — THE HONEST CHECK: DOES THE CO-OPTING SMUGGLE?

5.1 The question

  • e co-opting is rhetorically powerful, but is it LOGICALLY valid, or does it smuggle in the Śaiva
  • taphysics?

5.2 The honest analysis

  • e co-opting is valid at a specific level and smuggles at another.
  • Valid:** it shows the Buddhist cannot use the dream/inference/self-awareness to conclude unreality or
  • -self WITHOUT also licensing the Śaiva reading. The Buddhist's arguments are under-determined — they
  • pport idealism/self-awareness but not specifically the Buddhist's conclusion. The co-opting blocks the
  • ddhist's negative conclusion.
  • Smuggling:** the leap from "the appearances are self-articulating" to "there is ONE universal
  • nsciousness that creates" is NOT entailed by the co-opting. The dream shows a consciousness can
  • eate an object-mass; it does not show there is one universal creator. The co-opting establishes
  • nsciousness-as-fundamental; the universality is the additional commitment (the same gap that runs
  • rough the whole system).

5.3 The verdict

"The co-opting establishes consciousness-as-fundamental; the universality is the separate commitment —
the same gap as the reflexion-core and the felt→ground crux." (the co-opting session)
  • e co-opting is valid against the Buddhist's negative conclusion (the dream/inference/self-awareness
  • not prove unreality or no-self) but smuggles the positive Śaiva conclusion (one universal creator)
  • at the co-opting does not entail. This is the honest boundary, and it is the same in every document of

PART VI — THE VALENCE OF THE SAME APPEARANCES (THE SYNTHESIS)

6.1 The deepest insight

  • e co-opting reveals that the Buddhist and the Śaiva are not two opposing systems but TWO READINGS OF
  • E SAME STARTING POINT. Both begin from appearances (ābhāsa) as all we have. The Buddhist reads them
  • gatively (unreal, no-self, empty); the Śaiva reads them positively (the real self-articulation of
  • nsciousness).
  • The debate is not a clash of worldviews but a dispute over the VALENCE of the same appearances.** The
  • ddhist is not the enemy of the recognition-thesis but its co-owner of the starting point — the one who
  • ads the same data negatively.

6.2 The two idealisms, compared

  • Theme | Vijñānavāda | IPVV (Pratyabhijñā) |
  • ------|-------------|---------------------|
  • Starting point | appearances (ābhāsa) as all we have | appearances (ābhāsa) as all we have |
  • The object | unreal (no external thing) | real as the ground of the form (the arpaka) |
  • The self | no-self (momentary stream) | the non-constructed "I" (V2L) |
  • The appearances | unreal, empty | the real self-articulation of consciousness |
  • The dream | proof of unreality | proof of the creation-power |
  • Self-awareness | svasamvedana (adopted) | the self-luminous cognition (deepened, V2C) |
  • The valence | negative | positive |

6.3 The convergence on self-awareness

  • e two idealisms share the crucial claim of self-awareness (svasamvedana). The Buddhist holds cognition
  • self-aware; the Śaiva deepens it. And the difference is the valence: for the Buddhist, the
  • lf-awareness is momentary and empty; for the Śaiva, it is the felt self-grasp that is the essence of
  • nsciousness and the root of the recognition. The co-opting (V2C) takes the shared self-awareness and
  • ves it the positive reading.

PART VII — THE COMPARATIVE VERDICT

7.1 The co-opting as the Śaiva method

  • e IPVV's method against the Buddhist is the co-opting: accept the Buddhist's own tools (inference, the
  • eam, self-awareness) and turn them to the Śaiva conclusion. This is not refutation; it is absorption.
  • d it reveals the deepest fact about the two idealisms: they are two readings of the same appearances,
  • ffering in valence.

7.2 The honest boundary

  • e co-opting validly blocks the Buddhist's negative conclusion, but it smuggles the positive
  • iversalization. The dream proves a consciousness creates; it does not prove one universal creator.
  • e felt→ground step — from the per-field consciousness to the one — is the commitment, and the Buddhist
  • ightly, from its own premises) declines it. The two idealisms share the starting point and diverge on
  • e valence; the Śaiva's positive universalization is the wager.

7.3 The significance

  • e comparison is important because it shows the recognition-thesis is not a refutation of Buddhism but
  • re-valence of it. The Buddhist's tools are not destroyed; they are adopted and turned. The
  • cognition-thesis is the Buddhist's own starting point, read positively — the appearances as the real
  • lf-articulation of consciousness, and the self-awareness as the felt self-grasp. And the one thing the
  • o cannot share is the valence: the Buddhist reads the appearances as unreal, the Śaiva as real. That
  • lence — and the universalization that goes with it — is the Śaiva commitment.
